data.name: Monsterland
data.detailed_description:
To Desura users who spent money on "Dead Colony"

Send us your Desura receipt at founder@secondvarietygames.com , and you will get a free Steam key for "Mutant Gate", because "Mutant Gate" is an upgraded and revised version of "Dead Colony".


Acerca do jogo

After 10 years of sleep, Dr. Green wakes up in cryoprison on an Earth colony overrun by Mutants (former humans). Green has a past to atone for, but he also must find his estranged daughter Anna. On his way through the ravaged planet, he will be faced with intense combat, encounter survivors, and feel the wind of adventure. Will this story have a happy ending?
...
Monsterland is written on its own ASCII engine, its 4-hour campaign featuring a multitude of scripted sequences within 2D, Doom-style levels. There's also an option for hybrid ASCII/tile visuals. The game auto-detects Steam Deck and supports its controls.

data.short_description: After years in cryoprison, Dr. Green awakens on a mutant-infested Earth colony. Seeking redemption and his estranged daughter Anna, he battles through a ravaged planet in a 4-hour campaign of intense combat, encounters, and adventure. Monsterland has hybrid tile/ASCII visuals & Steam Deck support.

reviews.review:
Monsterland is an unconventional action adventure that embraces minimalism as its defining feature rather than treating it as a limitation. Developed and published by Second Variety Games, it presents a post-apocalyptic shooting experience through ASCII characters, symbols, simple tiles, and strong color contrasts. The unusual appearance immediately gives the game an identity of its own, but beneath that experimental exterior is a recognizable old-school action game built around exploration, combat, resource collection, and carefully arranged levels.

The campaign follows Dr. Green, who awakens after spending ten years in cryoprison and discovers that the colony around him has fallen into ruin. A medical drug intended to benefit humanity instead produced disastrous consequences, transforming people into dangerous mutants and leaving civilization devastated. Green's journey is not motivated solely by survival, as he is also searching for his estranged daughter, Anna. That personal objective gives the adventure a clearer sense of direction and provides some narrative weight to an otherwise straightforward mutant-shooting premise.

Gameplay takes inspiration from classic shooters while translating their ideas into a real-time 2D format. Instead of navigating three-dimensional corridors from a first-person viewpoint, players explore environments from a more abstract perspective, fighting mutants and searching for whatever is required to continue deeper into the colony. Combat happens in real time, making Monsterland much more immediate than its ASCII appearance might suggest. It may visually resemble the kind of game associated with slow, turn-based dungeon exploration, but its actual rhythm is closer to an arcade shooter.

Learning to interpret the screen is part of the experience. Enemies, environmental features, blood, objects, and other details are communicated through symbols and colors rather than elaborate artwork. Initially, this can make the world harder to understand because players must develop familiarity with its visual language. Once that adjustment occurs, however, the minimal presentation becomes surprisingly functional. There is also a hybrid ASCII and tile-based graphical option for players who want greater visual clarity without completely abandoning the game's distinctive style.

The handcrafted nature of the campaign is particularly important. Monsterland does not simply depend on procedural generation to manufacture endless rooms. Its environments contain deliberately arranged situations and scripted sequences, allowing encounters to feel more purposeful. Exploring an area, discovering supplies, encountering survivors, and suddenly dealing with hostile creatures gives the journey a stronger sense of progression than its primitive-looking presentation might initially imply. The design frequently feels like classic shooter philosophy reduced to its most fundamental elements.

Monsterland is also relatively compact, with its campaign designed to last around four hours. That duration works in its favor because the central mechanics are enjoyable but not especially deep. Combat and exploration provide enough entertainment for a focused adventure, although players expecting complicated character development, extensive equipment systems, elaborate builds, or dozens of hours of content may find the experience limited. The game understands its scale and generally avoids extending its mechanics beyond what they can comfortably support.

Atmosphere is another surprisingly effective component. The ruined colony, mutated inhabitants, isolated survivors, and Green's search for his daughter create a bleak science-fiction setting despite the lack of conventional visual detail. In some ways, the abstraction encourages imagination because the player mentally interprets symbols as locations, creatures, violence, and environmental destruction. Blood and combat are represented through the same minimalist visual language, allowing the game to communicate brutality without depending on realistic gore.

The audiovisual and technical presentation naturally remains modest. Monsterland was designed to operate on very lightweight hardware, and its storage requirements are tiny compared with most modern games. That makes it accessible on a broad range of computers while reinforcing the deliberately retro philosophy behind the project. Steam achievements and Steam Cloud functionality provide some additional conveniences, but this is fundamentally a straightforward single-player experience rather than a game built around extensive progression systems or online features.

Steam Deck compatibility is somewhat unusual. The game does not currently carry an official Steam Deck Verified or Playable classification, so its formal compatibility status should be considered Unknown or Unverified. However, the game was designed to detect the Steam Deck and provide control support for the handheld. Players should therefore distinguish between the absence of Valve's official compatibility badge and the presence of developer-supported Deck controls. Individual configurations can still produce differences, but the lightweight technical requirements make the game a reasonable candidate for handheld play.

Its biggest weakness is also inseparable from its greatest strength. ASCII graphics create a memorable identity, but they inevitably sacrifice immediate readability and conventional visual appeal. Some players will enjoy deciphering this strange world, while others may find the presentation unnecessarily difficult to follow. Combat is entertaining without becoming mechanically sophisticated, and the short campaign leaves relatively little room for substantial evolution. Replay value will consequently depend heavily on how much someone enjoys the distinctive presentation and straightforward action.

Despite those limitations, Monsterland succeeds as a compact experiment that turns ASCII graphics into the foundation of a functioning real-time action adventure. The combination of mutant combat, handcrafted environments, scripted moments, exploration, a personal storyline, and an unapologetically unusual graphical style gives it considerably more character than its simple appearance suggests. It will appeal most strongly to players interested in experimental indie games, retro shooters, minimalist graphics, and unusual interpretations of familiar genres.

Rating: 710
